Pele Yoetz 198:55: [23] Positive and negative commandments from the Torah that depend on the feet: It is a commandment to stand fully upright before one's father or mother. Rav Yosef, who was blind, used to say, when he heard the sound of his mother's footsteps, “Let me rise before the Divine Presence that is coming” (Kiddushin 31b). And even a hundred times a day one is obligated to rise before them, and likewise for one's grandfather and grandmother, one's mother's husband, one's father's wife and the like, one is obligated to rise before them. And included in honoring father and mother is that when his father or mother sends him for something, he must go and run at once with alacrity. It is a commandment to rise fully upright before a Torah scholar when he comes within his four cubits, even if he is not elderly. It is a commandment to rise fully upright before an elder of sixty years or more, and one accustomed to these commandments will merit the fear of Heaven. It is a commandment to rise before a Torah scroll. It is a commandment, when one comes to testify, to testify standing. It is a commandment to visit the sick and to strive to provide for their every need, and whoever does not visit the sick is as though he sheds blood. It is a commandment to accompany a person setting out on a journey, and whoever does not accompany him is as though he sheds blood. And whoever is accompanied, even four cubits within the city, will not come to harm, and the reward for this is without measure. It is a commandment to accompany the dead until burial, and whoever sees the dead and does not accompany him at least four cubits, his punishment is great, as one who curses and blasphemes the Lord. It is a commandment to stand while praying the Amidah, and likewise the commandments of the Omer count, tzitzit, and the shofar blasts require standing. A hint for this: “the counsel of the Lord stands forever.” The commandment of chalitzah.
Pele Yoetz 198:56: Negative commandments: Not to go outside the [Shabbat] boundary, that is, beyond two thousand cubits from the city on Shabbat. Not to return to dwell in the land of Egypt. Not to bow down to idolatry, and included in this: not to pray in a house containing an idol while facing the idol; not to bow toward a gentile who is wearing an idol; not to bend one's body to enter the doorway of a house containing an idol, but rather to enter backward; and not to bend down to pick up something that fell before an idol, but rather to turn one's back to the idol [while picking it up]. Not to prostrate oneself on a stone floor before the blessed Name anywhere except in the Temple; and full prostration with arms and legs outstretched is forbidden by Torah law, while prostration without arms and legs outstretched is forbidden by rabbinic law. Therefore mats or boards should be spread in synagogues that are paved with stone.
Pele Yoetz 198:57: [24] Positive and negative commandments from the words of Kabbalah and the words of the Sages that depend on the feet: It is a commandment to run to the synagogue and the study hall and to any matter of a commandment, even on Shabbat. It is a commandment to be counted among the first ten in the synagogue. It is a commandment to fix a place for one's prayer. It is a commandment to keep one's feet together during prayer and when responding to Kedushah. It is a commandment to bend the knees at the beginning and end of the first blessing [Avot], at the beginning and end of Hoda'ah [thanksgiving], and at Oseh Shalom, and together with the cantor at Modim. It is a commandment to take three steps backward at Oseh Shalom, like one taking leave from before the King. It is a commandment to stand for the blessing of the New Moon, which is like receiving the presence of the Divine Presence. It is a commandment to greet one's teacher on the festival. It is a commandment to greet one's teacher and friend who has returned from a journey. It is a commandment to go to a house of mourning to console the mourner. It is a commandment to go to a wedding feast. One must make the effort to walk four mil so as not to pray alone but rather with ten, and if he needs to detour from his path, he must go up to a mil out of his way, and likewise to obtain water for washing hands before prayer. It is a commandment to run to greet the kings of the nations of the world, so that if he merits it, he may distinguish [the honor due the King of kings by comparison]. One must cease associating with an angry person, distance oneself from a bad neighbor, and not associate with a wicked person (Avot 1:7). One who has distress or illness in his household should go to a sage and ask him to pray for mercy on his behalf, as it is said (Proverbs 16:14), “The king's wrath is like messengers of death, but a wise man will pacify it.”
Pele Yoetz 198:58: Negative commandments: It is forbidden to take large steps when leaving the synagogue. It is forbidden to take large steps on Shabbat (Shabbat 113b), and even on a weekday it is not [fully] permitted. The Holy One, blessed be He, hates one who enters his own house suddenly, and all the more so his fellow's house. Once the Torah scroll has been opened, it is forbidden to leave except between one reader's aliyah and the next, and of one who leaves it is said (Isaiah 1:28), “And those who forsake the Lord shall be consumed.” It is forbidden to sit or pass in front of someone praying until one has distanced oneself four cubits (Berachot 27a, 31b). It is forbidden to pass behind the synagogue while the congregation is praying, due to the appearance of impropriety. It is forbidden to walk four cubits without washing one's hands after sleeping. It is forbidden to walk four cubits with an upright bearing or bareheaded, for the whole earth is full of His glory. It is a great commandment to cherish the Land of Israel and to come to it from the ends of the earth with great longing, like a son to his mother's bosom.
Pele Yoetz 198:59: [25] Positive commandments from the Torah that depend on the private organ: It is a commandment to circumcise one's son. It is a commandment to circumcise converts. It is a commandment to betroth a woman with money, a document, or intercourse (Kiddushin 2a). The commandment of procreation. And if he had children who died, he has not fulfilled his duty unless, at the time of his death, he leaves behind from his own issue a son and a daughter. It is a commandment to fulfill one's conjugal duty for the sake of Heaven. It is a commandment for a man to separate from his wife near the time of her menstrual period. If he was with his ritually pure wife and she sensed that she had begun to menstruate, it is her duty to tell him, and it is forbidden for him to move or to withdraw while still aroused, but rather he must wait until the arousal subsides. It is a commandment for a man to separate from his wife if he found in her a matter of immorality. It is a commandment for one who divorces to give a bill of divorce in accordance with the law of Moses and Israel. The commandment of levirate marriage. It is a commandment to sanctify oneself even in what is permitted to him — not to be a glutton and a drunkard, and not to be obsessed with the world's delicacies, and to guard himself even in permitted speech; and he should not be obsessed with his wife and constantly with her like roosters, but rather minimize marital relations, engaging in them only as much as is needed to fulfill the commandment. It is a commandment for the kohanim to be holy and to separate from the women forbidden to them.
Pele Yoetz 198:60: [26] Negative commandments from the Torah that depend on the private organ: Not to come near any of the forbidden relations. It is forbidden to marry off one's daughter to an old man, for this causes her to stray. One who rapes a woman may not divorce the woman he raped. One who defames [his wife with a false accusation] may not divorce his wife. One who performs chalitzah may not marry the woman on whom he performed chalitzah. One who divorces may not remarry his wife after she has married or become betrothed to another. A mamzer may not marry a daughter of Israel. An Israelite may not marry a mamzeret. A eunuch may not marry a daughter of Israel. Not to have relations with a gentile woman, and of one who has relations with a gentile woman it is written (Malachi 2:12), “May the Lord cut off the man who does this,” and zealots may attack him. And in the Zohar (Shemot, p. 3) this sin is treated more stringently than all other forbidden relations (and woe to those found [doing so] in the lands of Edom — may the good Lord grant atonement). Not to commit adultery with oneself, that is, rubbing one's member with the hand or foot and destroying the seed. One who does this is considered a murderer and liable to death. This was the sin of Er and Onan and the sin of the generation of the Flood, and he is under a ban according to the sages of Israel. It is forbidden to be secluded with a woman forbidden to him among the forbidden relations, whether old or young. Not to engage in male intercourse, and both the active and passive participants are liable to stoning. One who withholds his major bodily functions transgresses “do not make yourselves detestable” (Makkot 16b), and regarding minor functions, both “do not make yourselves detestable” and “there shall be no infertile one among you” (Deuteronomy 7:14), for withholding poses great danger of infertility. One must not delay even a moment, so as not to become a cause preventing the fulfillment of the commandment to be fruitful and multiply, which would be a criminal sin.
Pele Yoetz 198:61: Every sin of forbidden relations is exceedingly grave and too great to bear, and wherever you find a fence against immorality, you find holiness. And the fence in the matter of forbidden relations must be to purify thought, speech, deed, sight, and hearing, and to distance oneself greatly from every hint of prohibition, at which point one will be holy.
Pele Yoetz 198:62: [27] Positive and negative commandments from the words of Kabbalah and the words of the Sages that depend on the private organ: It is a commandment to fulfill one's wife's conjugal needs when she longs for her husband, and especially at the time he sets out on a journey and when he returns from a journey. If he had children in his youth, he should have children in his old age too, for you do not know which will succeed. A bride [married] without a blessing is forbidden to her husband like a niddah (beginning of Tractate Kallah). It is forbidden to have relations against his wife's will. It is forbidden to have relations without shelter, in an open field. It is forbidden to have relations during the day. It is forbidden to have relations by candlelight, for [it is said] the children born from this will be epileptic. It is forbidden to have relations without covering the body, out of modesty. It is forbidden to have relations in the presence of any living creature. Rather, one should conduct himself with modesty and holiness, and thereby his offspring will be holy seed, whom all who see them will recognize as seed that the Lord has blessed.
Pele Yoetz 198:63: [28] Let the power of the Lord be magnified as a person accustoms himself to study these matters every day, as a reminder before his eyes, to keep, do and fulfill them, and let him at least not let a full week, or at least a full month, pass without this trustworthy reading. And especially must the Torah scholar be careful in all his affairs, that nothing improper or uncorrected come from his hand, for his unwitting errors are treated as deliberate sins. Also the grave sin of desecrating God's Name attaches to this. And whoever is greater [in stature] has a greater inclination [against him], and must build a fence, a hedge, and a safeguard for the safeguard, and a reminder. Therefore let the righteous man hold to his way and act as is fitting for him, according to what he needs. Let the wise man hear and add learning.
Pele Yoetz 199:1: Letter Lamed: Limud (Study) — The saying of the Tanna is known (Avot 2:16): “Study Torah much, and much reward will be given you.” Indeed, the order of study is a straight path that a person should choose for himself. Since Torah study must be for its own sake, in order to fulfill, keep, and do, thus a person should divide his hours each day, and whoever the Lord has graced with understanding should fix a time for close analysis in halachah, or in the halachic authorities, with depth and dialectic according to his ability, and if he can study with colleagues or with good students, how good and pleasant that is. He should also fix times to study for expertise, and let his study begin with the laws needed in the Shulchan Aruch together with all the later authorities, until they are fixed in his mind for when needed, and then return to study systematically all of the twenty-four books of Scripture with Rashi's commentary, and the Mishnayot with commentary, and the entire Talmud with Rashi and Tosafot, and the fourteen sections of the Rambam with the commentaries, and the four Turim with the commentaries, and likewise the four sections of the Shulchan Aruch, and afterward other studies and knowledge, until he is complete in knowledge. And the study of ethical books and the fear of the Lord rises above all these like the spices added to every food. And after he has filled his stomach with all the studies and knowledge according to the plain meaning, let him strive to study the wisdom of Kabbalah, for it is known that on the Day of Judgment a person is also asked about the mysteries of the Torah and the workings of the divine Chariot (Midrash Mishlei, ch. 10), and he will be held accountable in the future if he was able to study and did not. And one accustomed to the Zohar will see how much shame comes in the World to Come to one who did not study the wisdom of Kabbalah, to the point that they said in several places that it would have been better for him not to have been created — it makes a person's hair stand on end. And certainly the Holy One, blessed be He, does not deal tyrannically with His creatures (Avodah Zarah 3a), and all according to what the person is, it is incumbent upon him to attain as much knowledge as is in his power, and he should not turn to idleness even for a moment, for the day is short and the work is much.
Pele Yoetz 199:2: And even one whom the Lord has not graced with understanding has no basis for exemption on the Day of Judgment by saying, “I have recited all of Psalms and reviewed eighteen chapters of Mishnah and several pages of the holy Zohar — what more is my duty? Could I possibly keep going over Psalms and the like and sit and study all day? This is impossible.” I say that this too is mere vanity spoken by their mouths, and woe to people from the Day of Judgment and the depth of judgment, for even one who has studied the entire Torah is not permitted to sit idle or engage in idle talk even for a moment, and God will bring everything into judgment, and one will be held accountable in the future even for the brief time it takes to swallow saliva, as is known from the saying of our sages, of blessed memory. And they said (Tanna DeVei Eliyahu, ch. 2) that even one who studies all day the verse “and Timna was the sister of Lotan” comes to his reward as one who studies the laws of leprosy and tent-impurity, and both the one who does much and the one who does little [are equal], provided he directs his heart to Heaven (Berachot 5b). And a man who fears for his soul on the great and awesome Day of Judgment should not follow the majority for evil, but rather heed the words of our holy sages, and strive with all his might to find rest for his soul and to satisfy his soul with delights, and when he sits to study, let him guard his soul so as not to inherit a double Gehinnom, and let his study be for the sake of keeping, doing and fulfilling, and let him not labor in vain, but rather study aloud, in clear speech, to give delight to his Maker, and not interrupt his study for idle matters, and pay attention to understand what he is studying. And it is known that the Holy One, blessed be He, counts not pages but hours, and a little with proper intention is better.
Pele Yoetz 200:1: Lev (Heart) — A good heart is what all of Judaism and all service of the blessed Name depends upon. And the saying of the Tanna is known, who said (Avot 2:9), “I regard the words of Rabbi Elazar ben Arach as superior to your words,” for his words included your words. And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 106b, with Rashi) that the Merciful One desires the heart. There are commandments that depend on the heart and are constant, which one can fulfill at every time and every moment, such as to fear and to love the honored and awesome Lord and to cling to Him and to fulfill “I have set the Lord before me always” (Psalms 16:8); and beyond this, all six hundred and thirteen commandments depend on the heart, for a person should take to heart what these commandments are and what reason lies in them, and how they should properly be performed with fear, love and great joy, and how one should overcome his inclination so as not to transgress his Maker's will and not to anger his Creator, and how one should strengthen himself to fulfill every commandment properly and not retreat before anything — not because of the trouble, not because of the cold, not because of the shame, and not because of the expense — and how one should distance himself from all bad and deficient traits and conduct himself with good traits, and weigh the loss of a commandment against its reward and the reward of a transgression against its loss, and consider what his duty is and do it, and reflect on the greatness of the Creator and His goodness and kindnesses toward him, and consider the greatness of his own wrongdoing in angering his Creator, and humble his heart with great humility. All this and more should a living person take to heart, to keep, do, and fulfill every good thing, and to guard against every bad thing.
Pele Yoetz 200:2: And it is also a duty of the heart to have intention in prayers and blessings and studies and the meaning of the words, and before whom he stands and with whom he speaks, and to whom he is blessing, and how good is our portion and how pleasant our lot, that He chose us as a treasured people, a great and awesome King. And if he knows how to have the [Kabbalistic] intentions and unifications and the pairings of the supernal attributes, happy is he and happy is his portion.
Pele Yoetz 200:3: It is also a duty of the heart to consider how to conduct oneself with people, and to despise honor and all the pleasures and vanities of this world, for it is all vanity and emptiness, and to delight in doing his Maker's will and to trust in Him truly. And to believe in Him with complete faith and in His providence, that He watches over the smallest of details, and that whatever happens to him, whether by the hand of Heaven or by human hands, whether for good or for what seems otherwise, all is from Him for his benefit. What can be said — the mouth cannot speak nor can words describe the greatness of the duties of the heart. The end of the matter, all having been heard (Ecclesiastes 12:13), for this is a great principle of the Torah and this is the whole of man. Happy is the man who fears the Lord and reflects deeply to think pure thoughts and joins a good thought to deed. Happy is he in this world and it is well with him in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 201:1: Lashon HaRa (Slander) — The evil of slander is well known to be so great that they said (Arachin 15b) that it is equal to idolatry, illicit relations, and bloodshed, and King David, peace be upon him, already cut it off. Slander is speaking ill of one's fellow, even if speaking the truth, and it is a sin from which no one who does not take it to heart is saved, for whoever multiplies words brings about sin. And it is written (Psalms 34:13-14), “Who is the man who desires life... guard your tongue from evil.” And from the severity of its punishment we can learn how much it angers his Creator. Therefore let a man be firm in strengthening himself to stand guard and keep a muzzle on his mouth, and make himself like a mute regarding speaking of his fellow, whether good or bad. And the pain is even greater regarding those who speak ill of a family, or of the people of a city, or of a tribe of Israel, such as Sephardim against Ashkenazim and Ashkenazim against Sephardim.
Pele Yoetz 201:2: And it is known from the words of our sages, of blessed memory, that the Holy One, blessed be He, is very strict with those who teach a case against Israel, for there is no city, family, tribe, or individual person that does not have some grain and straw mixed in, and there is no tree without smoke, and none is complete in everything except the One, unique and singular, may His Name be blessed; and people have no right to disparage anyone for having something not good found in him, for a man's way is right in his own eyes, and what can the child do — whatever is right in his own eyes he does according to his own understanding and whatever help he has from the Almighty.
Pele Yoetz 201:3: Moreover, one should not condemn an entire family or an entire city because of a few of their members found to have done wrong. And if the punishment for slander against an individual is great, how much more so is the doubled and redoubled evil of speaking against the many. (And truly this requires study in light of what is found in the Talmud (Pesachim 50b) in several places disparaging the people of Choza'ah, who were indulgent, and what they said (Chullin 127a), “Who gave you a kiss” and the like. It is possible that there are grounds for permitting this, such as regarding something already publicly known, or in the manner of what they said (Yoma 86b), that it is a commandment to publicize hypocrites, or in the manner of what they said (Yerushalmi Pe'ah 1:1) that it is permitted to speak slander against those who foster strife. Nevertheless,) given the severity involved and the greatness of its punishment — from which we may deduce how greatly it angers his Creator — let a man tremble and take hold of himself, and flee a hundred gates of the permitted so as not to enter even one gate of the forbidden, and let him fear this more and more as before a sword, for even a doubt regarding danger to life overrides the entire Torah, and if the Torah is overridden for a mere doubt of temporary life, how much more so should optional matters be overridden even for a remote doubt, one in a thousand, for the sake of eternal life, and so as not to anger his Creator, the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He. And this is a great principle regarding every matter of transgression: to flee from a transgression and even from a doubtful transgression as from a sword, and not to enter into narrow loopholes seeking grounds for leniency, but rather let all his bones tremble from fear of the Lord and the majesty of His grandeur. Happy is the man who fears the Lord, and let these matters, and this and that, be a remembrance before his eyes, so that he be remembered as righteous forever.
Pele Yoetz 201:4: And since the great obligation of the commandment of rebuke is known, and it is known that whoever's ears hear forbidden words are also burned by them, thus it is fitting for those who fear the Lord and esteem His Name, when standing among gatherings of unlearned people in their synagogues who talk excessively — which is included in slander, which through our sins has become as though fully permitted, with no one taking care to be wary, since they do not know what slander is — it is fitting to warn them and remind them and say to the speaker, “Enough of this slander” (Bava Batra 164b), and likewise regarding every transgression one sees in others. Let him be firm in strengthening himself to have regard for his Maker's honor and for his own soul, and tell them their transgression and the house of Jacob their sins, and thereby he redeems his own soul, as I shall write further, God willing, under the entries Rebuke and Sin.
Pele Yoetz 202:1: Leitzanut (Mockery) — The severity of its prohibition is known, to the point that they said (Avodah Zarah 18b) that its beginning is suffering and its end is destruction. And many other evils befall the mocker, as explained in the words of our holy sages, of blessed memory. The matter of mockery is that one mocks his fellow to increase laughter and levity, and this sin is found in abundance, especially in the orders of Nashim and Nezikin [of the Mishnah, whose subject matter lends itself to jesting], even unknowingly, since people do not know its prohibition and severity, and do not know to be careful about it except for a few survivors.
Pele Yoetz 202:2: Indeed, there is a chronic evil from which almost no one is saved, and it is the saying of our sages, of blessed memory (Avot 3:2): two who sit together without words of Torah between them — this is a session of scoffers. Even schoolchildren know this, for they read Pirkei Avot in the synagogue, yet no one takes it to heart to be careful. And God will bring everything into judgment — whether one believes the words of our sages, of blessed memory, and does not fulfill them, or does not believe them at all; and woe to whoever can survive when God's judgment arises. And behold, there are lighter transgressions that people are careful about, while with graver transgressions it is as though we have become so rooted in them that the prohibition is no longer recognizable to us, and it is even considered in our eyes a commandment to mingle with people [in idle talk], and no one feels pain over it or takes to heart to repent. Whoever desires life, let a man be firm in strengthening himself with valor, not merely with strength.
Pele Yoetz 203:1: Lishmah (For Its Own Sake) — The saying of the Tanna Rabbi Meir is known: whoever engages in Torah for its own sake merits many things (Avot 6:1; Kallah, beginning of ch. 8). And our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital, may his memory be for a blessing, already wrote that if the Torah scholars of our time were to say they engage in Torah for its own sake, the great Tanna Rabbi Meir would contradict them, for he said that whoever engages in Torah for its own sake merits many things, and there is not even one who merits all of them, or even part of them.
Pele Yoetz 203:2: There are several kinds of “not for its own sake.” There is one who acts so that people will praise and extol his deeds, and his whole aim is this, so that he constantly says “we must be praised”, and he engages in Torah and commandments only in public, out of fear and honor, but when alone he becomes a different person, his deeds strange, his service foreign. Such a man should be called a hypocrite and a flatterer, and his wickedness is great, for he acts as though the eye above does not see, and increases the honor of the servant more than the honor of his Master, and woe to him, for he will also be punished regarding his commandments and Torah, and will be shamed and disgraced like the shame of a thief, for this is nothing but deceiving people's minds.
Pele Yoetz 203:3: And there is one who does not act specifically so that people will praise him, and he is God-fearing both in private and in public, but it pleases him if the matter becomes known to the public through some cause, so that they come to know that he has done good, and his heart rejoices within him. This too is vanity and vexation of spirit, for a person must fulfill “walk humbly with your God” as much as possible, so that his deeds be specifically for the sake of Heaven. And if it happens that others learn of the matter and praise him, and the nearby inclination entices him with a double enticement to enjoy it and let his heart be lifted up, let him immediately seek escape for himself and reason: what does it give me and what does it add to me if people, who are like a breath, praise me or disparage me? And if they praise and honor me, thinking I have done a great thing, do I not know myself that I should not take credit for myself, for this is the very purpose for which I was created, and I have not yet done even one part in a thousand thousand of what is incumbent on me to do, in accordance with the goodness and kindness the Lord has bestowed upon me — the greatest kindness being that He has increased His goodness toward me and graced me with understanding and given me the merit to perform this commandment. How shall I repay the Lord for this? I am unworthy of all the kindnesses and all the truth, and therefore
Pele Yoetz 203:4: let me bow before the God on high, who has helped me until now, and let him feel great pain over even a moment's arrogance of heart, lest, God forbid, he be included among those of whom it is said, “every haughty heart is an abomination to the Lord,” and let him quickly find escape for himself and humble his heart.
Pele Yoetz 203:5: And there is yet another manner of “not for its own sake,” such as one who acts in order to have a good reward for his labor in the World to Come, or in order to be saved from rebuke for sin. And of this they said (Pesachim 50b): a person should always engage in Torah and commandments even not for their own sake, for from [engaging] not for its own sake one comes to [engage] for its own sake — for as his body is purified through performing the commandments and his soul becomes pure, then he will have help from the Almighty to fulfill [Torah study] for its own sake. However, the essential service must be for its own sake, for otherwise, it turns out that he is not serving his Creator but rather himself, for his own pleasure and benefit.
Pele Yoetz 203:6: Behold, the matter of “for its own sake” is that one engages in Torah in order to keep, fulfill, and correct matters as ordained in the supernal realm, to give delight to our Creator. And when a person reflects deeply in the depths of his heart's thoughts on the loftiness of our God's greatness, and what is man that He is mindful of him, he will know and his heart will understand that there is no good greater in this world and the World to Come than serving God and giving Him delight, and “better is one hour of Torah and good deeds in this world than all the life of the World to Come” (Avot 4:17). And it is fitting for a person to say: if the Holy One, blessed be He, in His kindness and compassion wishes to give me reward for the Torah and good deeds that I do, my wish is that my reward be only that He grant me the merit and help me further to do His will as He wills, to give delight before His Throne of Glory, for there is no reward better or greater than this.
Pele Yoetz 203:7: And this, in my opinion, is the intent of what we say in the Amidah prayer: “Give good reward to all who truly trust in Your Name, and place our portion among them,” for the good reward is doing His will, blessed and exalted be His Name. Behold, consider how much joy and honor and greatness there is for a man if the king desires him and chooses him, subjugating him before himself favorably, even without money and without price — and how much more so if he is a lowly person, and the king desires his honor and honors and exalts him to serve before him — certainly this man's heart will rejoice and his glory will exult, and the whole world will call him happy and say of him, happy is he and happy is his portion. As for us, whom our Maker has chosen to serve before Him, to give delight before His Throne of Glory, how much more so is this a good beyond measure. And if a person gives his life to death in order to merit being destined for life in the World to Come, how much more fitting is it to accept even a thousand deaths in order to merit giving delight to the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He. This and more should he reflect upon deeply and lift his mind on high, until he subjugates his service into a complete service, a perfect service, with fear, love and great joy, and all his deeds should be for the sake of Heaven, and “one who comes to purify himself is helped from Heaven” (Shabbat 104a).
Pele Yoetz 204:1: Loveh (Borrower) — It is good for a man, from time to time, to borrow from his fellow in order to fulfill the commandment of repaying a debt. And likewise in several commandments, the God-fearing man, who delights in His commandments, seeks to bring himself under obligation and to fulfill them, and is thus found diligent and rewarded. But now many unlearned people transgress this commandment: when they do not have much surplus, they are not concerned to press themselves even a little in order to fulfill this commandment, and how many evils they cause thereby. One is that they lock the door before borrowers. Another is that the lender gnashes his teeth and is consumed when he sees his debtor having enough to eat his fill and to clothe himself, while he himself eats delicacies and dresses his wife and children in fine clothing, and he cannot restrain himself from crying out bitterly and uttering a fierce curse; and since one who borrows and does not repay is called wicked, as it is written (Psalms 37:21), “The wicked borrows and does not repay,” and one who borrows from a person is like one who borrows from the Omnipresent (Avot ch. 2, near end), it is fitting for a man to press himself and sell his belongings and everything he has in his house and repay his creditor, and it is better that he be cast into hunger, nakedness and lacking everything than to be wicked before the Omnipresent even for one hour. And how much more so if the lender himself is in pressing need, or if he is a Torah scholar — he should not delay paying them, for the Lord will plead their cause and will take away the life of those who rob them (Proverbs 22:23). And even if he is a wealthy man, if he can appease him with good words to wait, how good that is; and if not, let him sell his clothing and fulfill the commandment of repaying a debt.
Pele Yoetz 204:2: And it is already written in Sefer Chasidim (section 454) that one who has a creditor should not increase his charitable giving, and certainly should not increase his expenses, for the envy of the lender is as harsh as the grave, and his eye is evil regarding his own money, so that whatever he sees him eating and wearing, he will surely say, “It would have been better for him to pay me.” At the very least, let the borrower do this: repay little by little, for every penny adds to the account, and thereby appease his creditor, and let him be troubled and it will be well for him, and let him strive with all his might toward “increase repayment,” [as the mnemonic goes,] for one hour earlier is better, and thereby he will receive a blessing from the Lord, and the Lord will not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
Pele Yoetz 204:3: And this commandment is incumbent upon the heads and leaders of the city who sit on seats of judgment, not to show mercy in judgment but to rescue the exploited from the hand of his exploiter, and to collect even from the cloak on his shoulders; and if he shows a stubborn shoulder, they coerce him by every means of coercion, whether in Jewish courts or in gentile courts. And it is a duty incumbent on all Israel to stand at the right hand of the judges and to raise the banner of the Torah, and thereby they do a great good. One thing is that they save the borrower's soul from descending to the pit; and another is that the door not be locked before borrowers, and “the world is built on kindness.”
Pele Yoetz 205:1: La'az (Vernacular) — There are now many unlearned people who do not understand the Holy Tongue. And already many books in the vernacular have been written for the vernacular-speaking people, and furthermore, as long as the world lasts, whoever wishes to bring merit to Israel should devote himself to writing prayer orders, summaries of laws, and moral rebukes of practical wisdom in the vernacular, and this is better than publishing books of dialectics or homiletics, since those end up lying in a corner, benefiting only one person from a whole city, once in a jubilee; but books in the vernacular pass through the hands of many men and women. And there are men and women whose souls long to seek God and engage in the study that leads to practice, but their limited capacity prevents them from understanding and their hearts from grasping. Thus, those who write and print many books, new and old, in the vernacular, are the ones who bring merit to the many, and the merit of the many depends on them.
Pele Yoetz 205:2: And it is true that the special virtue of the Holy Tongue is great, to the point that they said that whoever can always speak even mundane matters in the Holy Tongue acquires holiness, and the matter is ancient. And in every single letter there are supernal mysteries, and he builds his chambers in heaven, and even if he does not know what he is saying, it is revealed before Heaven, and “the work of our hands, establish it for us.” But nonetheless there is a difference between one who understands what he says and one who does not understand, like the difference between light and darkness; therefore, there is a time for every desire — hold to this and also do not let go of that, for you do not know which will succeed, and therefore both together are good. And whoever desires life should pursue books that are beneficial for the healing and correction of the soul as one pursues a partridge in the mountains, for God will bring everything into judgment, including whether one was able to study and did not, and study is great when it leads to practice (Megillah 26a; Kiddushin 40b). (And I wished to write my own pamphlets, which I intended to benefit the many, in the vernacular, but because the Sephardic vernacular is not the same as that of Ashkenazim, Italians, and other language groups, I therefore chose the Holy Tongue, which is equal and beneficial for all languages, and I have left room for others, if they wish to bring merit to the many among the unlearned, to translate them into the vernacular of their own languages, as was done with the book “Shevet Musar,” and their reward will come doubled from Heaven.)
Pele Yoetz 206:1: Levayah (Accompanying) — Accompanying is an easy commandment, easy to perform, for by accompanying someone four cubits one has fulfilled the duty. Yet its punishment is severe, for one who does not accompany his fellow is as though he sheds blood. And many unlearned people are not careful about this, either from lack of knowledge or from inattention (though the wealthy have many friends who accompany them), and of such it is said (Isaiah 5:18), “Woe to those who drag sin with cords of falsehood.” And they said (Chagigah 5a), “Woe to us, for Scripture has weighed the light commandments as equal to the grave ones.” Whoever fears crossing [the line of transgression] should gird his loins like a man and not transgress any commandment, small or great, for you do not know the reward given for the commandments.
Pele Yoetz 207:1: Levishah (Dress) — It is known what they explained on the verse (Amos 4:12), “Prepare to meet your God” — that one must be properly dressed when standing in prayer (Shabbat 10a) or engaged in Torah, for the Divine Presence is before him. Even sitting alone in his house, he must sit as one standing before the ministers of the city, all according to local custom. And many transgress this when praying the evening prayer at home, or when engaged in Torah study at the first watch of the night. One must be very careful about this, as it is written (I Samuel 2:30), “For those who honor Me I will honor,” etc.
Pele Yoetz 207:2: And regarding clothing, it is fitting for a person to conduct himself moderately, according to what he is and according to the place, and even if the Lord has graced him with wealth, he should not wear extremely expensive embroidered garments — whether because he thereby transgresses “do not destroy,” or because he is thereby harming his own soul, since it brings a person to pride (a hint for this: “pride is clothed” [wordplay]), or because it arouses the evil inclination and the evil eye, or because it causes others who cannot afford it to see him and want to do as he does, and end up borrowing and not repaying, or robbing and stealing — and especially those women who abound in golden garments, silk and embroidery and expensive jewelry, various different kinds, causing harm to the world, for one woman envies another, and their whole aim is to resemble one another, and even if her husband's means are limited, he cannot avoid fulfilling his wife's wishes, for bad conduct in his household is hard to bear (Berachot 7b), and from this dowries and wedding expenses have multiplied, until many daughters come to disgrace upon reaching marriageable age unmarried, father and mother weeping and lamenting in raging distress, with no one to save them, and many such evils and troubles befall the heads of the poor — and what causes all this? The multiplication of expenses and permissive dress that have become the fixed norm.
Pele Yoetz 207:3: And it is fitting for community leaders to take this to heart and erect fences and enact ordinances for the settlement of the city and the betterment of the world. And we may learn from the elders, who enacted several ordinances for the sake of peace and for the betterment of the world. And in several places in the Talmud we find that they obligated the wealthy to be lenient regarding their own honor, so as not to shame the one who has nothing (Ta'anit 31a). And even a poor person should adorn himself with clean clothes, whatever he has; and “who can find a woman of valor” whose “watches over the ways of her household” ensures that her husband and children are not in torn or dirty clothes, for this is her honor and the honor of her children and husband, as Rabbi Yochanan called his garment “my honorer” (Shabbat 113b). And from this our sages, of blessed memory, explained what is written regarding Shabbat (Isaiah 58:13), “And you shall honor it” — honor it with clean clothing (Shabbat 119a).
Pele Yoetz 207:4: Happy is Israel, for even the poorest among them has a garment for Shabbat. But whoever has the means, how good and pleasant it is for him to fulfill the words of Rabbi Isaac Luria, of blessed memory, that he should have four white garments, and that he should also have a robe, trousers, and shoes for his feet, and even the cap he sleeps in should be designated specifically for Shabbat, in such a way that the mundane is not mixed at all with the holy. And part of being careful about this is that he put on his Shabbat clothes on the eve of Shabbat, and not approach receiving the sanctity and glory of Shabbat in weekday clothes, as is the custom of some people in certain places, for this is a bad custom, and the diligent hasten to perform commandments.
Pele Yoetz 207:5: Let one who is careful in his conduct be even more diligent to be careful and guard against the prohibition of sha'atnez, and investigate with seven inquiries and examinations regarding the sewing threads, for there is great potential for error among the threads with which garments are sewn with linen threads, and there are threads considered to be hemp that are actually pure linen, and one should not rely on presumption, but rather examine and investigate as far as possible, until it becomes completely clear to him that it is permissible. And a God-fearing person should fulfill all these requirements and sew his garments only with silk thread. And how good and pleasant is the custom of the pious of Ashkenaz, who do not wear woolen garments at all, since it commonly happens that the craftsman making the garment sometimes has it torn in the middle and sews it with linen thread, and this is something visible to the eye when the dye fades from the garment. And given the severity involved, extra care and diligence are required. Go and learn from the acronym [of sha'atnez] that it contains [the letters of] “Satan is bold,” and regarding this they already said that one who wears sha'atnez even for one hour, his prayer is not heard, God forbid. What are we and what is our life — therefore let every person be careful in his dress for the honor of the Rock of his sanctity.
Pele Yoetz 208:1: Desire, letter Mem: Malchut (Government) — It is known that it is a commandment from the words of Kabbalah to pray for the welfare of the government, for “were it not for the fear of it, men would swallow each other alive” (Avot 3:2). Therefore one must be careful to answer “Amen” after the blessing for the king that the prayer leader recites every Shabbat, in order to fulfill this commandment, and from this we may deduce that it is a commandment to pray for anyone from whom one derives benefit, and one should be accustomed to reciting this formula:
Pele Yoetz 208:2: May it be Your will, O Lord our God and God of our fathers, that all should strengthen our power, and that we have no accusers above and no adversaries below, and grant good reward to all who support us and all who benefit us. Bless, O Lord, their strength, and favor the work of their hands, and let them not be ashamed in this world, nor be disgraced in the World to Come.
